provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: WAEC marathon: mechanics
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to solve mechanics problems involving Newton's laws of motion, calculate work done and power in everyday situations, and identify sources of errors in measurement.

Introduction:
We have previously studied the fundamental principles of mechanics including Newton's laws and energy concepts. Today we will practice solving complex mechanics problems similar to those in WAEC examinations.

Content:
Mechanics problems in WAEC often involve motion, force, and energy. For example, a common problem might ask a student to calculate the work done when pushing a danfo bus with a force of 500N over a distance of 20m. Work done = force × distance = 500N × 20m = 10000J. Another example might involve calculating power when lifting a bag of rice weighing 100kg to a height of 2m in 5 seconds. Power = work/time = (mgh)/t = (100×10×2)/5 = 400W.

Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to solve 5 mechanics problems from past WAEC questions, identifying potential sources of error in each calculation and presenting their solutions to the class.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define work done in physics.
2. A boy pushes a wheelbarrow with a force of 100N over a distance of 50m. Calculate the work done.
3. Differentiate between kinetic and potential energy.
4. If a generator produces 5000J of energy in 10 seconds, what is its power rating?

Summary:
Today's practice has reinforced our understanding of mechanics principles and their application to solving examination problems.

topics.title: WAEC marathon: waves and light
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to draw and label diagrams of wave properties, calculate wave parameters, and explain applications of wave phenomena in everyday life.

Introduction:
We have previously studied the properties and behavior of waves and light. Today we will practice drawing wave diagrams and solving problems related to wave properties and optics.

Content:
Wave diagrams in WAEC often require students to show wavelength, amplitude, and frequency. For example, when drawing a transverse wave, students must clearly label these properties. A typical problem might ask students to calculate the frequency of a wave with wavelength 0.5m moving at 20m/s. Frequency = velocity/wavelength = 20/0.5 = 40Hz. For light, students must understand reflection and refraction. When light passes from air to water, it bends toward the normal because water has a higher refractive index.

Class activity:
Students will draw wave diagrams showing different types of waves and perform a practical demonstration of refraction using a glass block and laser pointer, measuring angles of incidence and refraction.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define wavelength and frequency of a wave.
2. A wave has a speed of 300m/s and a wavelength of 0.6m. Calculate its frequency.
3. Explain why a pencil appears bent when placed in a glass of water.
4. List two applications of ultrasound waves in medicine.

Summary:
Today's practice has improved our ability to visualize and calculate wave properties and understand optical phenomena.

topics.title: WAEC marathon: electricity
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to draw and interpret circuit diagrams, calculate electrical quantities using Ohm's law, and solve problems involving electrical power and energy.

Introduction:
We have previously studied electrical circuits, Ohm's law, and electrical power. Today we will practice solving complex circuit problems and calculating electrical quantities commonly found in WAEC examinations.

Content:
Electrical problems in WAEC often involve series and parallel circuits. For example, students may need to calculate the equivalent resistance of three resistors (2Ω, 3Ω, and 4Ω) in parallel. The formula for parallel resistance is 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3. Another common problem involves calculating power consumption. If an electric heater rated 1000V is used for 5 hours, the energy consumed is E = Pt = 1000W × 5h = 5kWh. Students must also be able to draw circuit symbols correctly for components like resistors, capacitors, and cells.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to construct simple series and parallel circuits using breadboards and measure voltage and current at different points using multimeters.

Evaluation questions:
1. State Ohm's law.
2. Three resistors of 2Ω, 4Ω, and 6Ω are connected in parallel. Calculate the equivalent resistance.
3. An electric bulb is rated 220V, 100W. Calculate the current through it when connected to the mains.
4. Differentiate between series and parallel circuits.

Summary:
Today's practice has strengthened our problem-solving skills in electrical circuits and our understanding of electrical quantities.

topics.title: WAEC marathon: heat
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state and apply gas laws, solve problems involving thermal expansion, and explain heat transfer mechanisms.

Introduction:
We have previously studied the kinetic theory of matter and thermal properties. Today we will practice solving problems involving gas laws and thermal concepts commonly tested in WAEC examinations.

Content:
Heat problems in WAEC often involve gas laws. For example, a typical question might ask what happens to the pressure of a gas when its volume is reduced by half at constant temperature. According to Boyle's law, pressure and volume are inversely proportional, so pressure doubles. Another common problem involves thermal expansion. If a steel rail of length 10m expands by 0.5cm when heated, the linear expansion coefficient can be calculated using ΔL = αLΔT. Students must also understand heat transfer - conduction in metal spoons, convection in boiling water, and radiation from the sun during harmattan season.

Class activity:
Students will perform an experiment to verify Charles' law by measuring the volume of air trapped in a capillary tube at different temperatures and plotting a graph of volume against temperature.

Evaluation questions:
1. State Boyle's law.
2. A gas occupies 2L at 27°C. What will be its volume at 127°C if pressure is constant?
3. Explain why a metal spoon gets hot when placed in hot water.
4. Calculate the linear expansion of a copper rod of length 5m when heated from 20°C to 80°C. (α for copper = 1.7×10^-5 K^-1)

Summary:
Today's practice has reinforced our understanding of gas laws and thermal properties with practical applications.

topics.title: WAEC marathon: modern physics
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain nuclear decay processes, solve problems involving half-life calculations, and discuss applications of nuclear physics.

Introduction:
We have previously studied atomic structure and nuclear reactions. Today we will practice solving problems involving nuclear physics and radioactivity commonly tested in WAEC examinations.

Content:
Modern physics problems in WAEC often involve radioactive decay and half-life calculations. For example, if a radioactive substance has a half-life of 10 years and initially contains 1000 atoms, after 30 years it will have 1000/(2^3) = 125 atoms remaining. Another common problem involves Einstein's mass-energy equivalence. If 1kg of mass is converted to energy, E = mc² = 1×(3×10^8)² = 9×10^16J. Students must also understand nuclear fission and fusion - the processes that power nuclear reactors and the sun respectively.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to research and present on different applications of nuclear physics in medicine, energy production, and everyday devices like smoke detectors.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define half-life of a radioactive substance.
2. A radioactive material has a half-life of 5 years. What fraction remains after 15 years?
3. Explain nuclear fission and give one example.
4. Calculate the energy released when 0.5kg of mass is converted to energy.

Summary:
Today's practice has enhanced our understanding of nuclear physics concepts and their applications in modern technology.

topics.title: Mock examination
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to demonstrate examination technique, apply physics principles to solve problems under timed conditions, and identify areas requiring further study.

Introduction:
We have covered all major topics in the physics syllabus. Today's mock examination will help you assess your preparedness for the actual WAEC examination by simulating exam conditions.

Content:
The mock examination will consist of two papers: Theory and Practical. The theory paper will include questions from all topics covered this term, with emphasis on mechanics, waves, electricity, heat, and modern physics. Questions will range from simple recall to complex problem-solving requiring multiple steps. The practical paper will involve experimental setup, measurement, and analysis of results. Students must manage their time effectively, allocating appropriate time to each section based on marks.

Class activity:
Students will write a full mock examination under timed conditions, followed by a review session where answers are discussed and common mistakes highlighted.

Evaluation questions:
The mock examination itself serves as the evaluation, with questions covering all topics and requiring both theoretical knowledge and problem-solving skills.

Summary:
Today's mock examination has provided valuable practice for the actual WAEC exam and highlighted areas requiring further revision.

topics.title: Practical marathon
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to set up physics experiments correctly, take accurate measurements, and present experimental results with proper analysis.

Introduction:
We have previously studied laboratory techniques and experimental procedures. Today we will practice WAEC-style practical physics experiments to improve our laboratory skills and experimental analysis.

Content:
WAEC practical physics typically involves experiments in mechanics, optics, electricity, and heat. For example, in an optics experiment, students might be asked to determine the focal length of a converging lens using the lens formula 1/f = 1/u + 1/v where u is object distance and v is image distance. In an electricity experiment, students might investigate the relationship between current and voltage for a resistor and determine its resistance. Students must learn to take readings carefully, repeat measurements for reliability, and identify sources of error such as parallax error when reading instruments.

Class activity:
Students will rotate through different experimental stations, performing tasks such as measuring the specific heat capacity of a solid, verifying Ohm's law, and determining the refractive index of a glass block.

Evaluation questions:
1. List two sources of error in an electrical experiment.
2. Explain how you would determine the focal length of a converging lens.
3. Why are multiple readings taken in an experiment?
4. Describe how to minimize parallax error when taking measurements.

Summary:
Today's practical exercises have enhanced our laboratory skills and improved our ability to handle experimental equipment and analyze results.

topics.title: Weakness clinics
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify their areas of weakness in physics, apply targeted strategies to improve these areas, and demonstrate improved problem-solving skills in previously challenging topics.

Introduction:
From our mock examinations and practical sessions, we have identified several areas where students commonly struggle. Today we will focus on these topics with targeted practice and remedial teaching.

Content:
Common weaknesses in physics problem-solving include mechanics involving inclined planes, electromagnetic induction, and nuclear calculations. For mechanics on inclined planes, students must resolve forces parallel and perpendicular to the plane. For example, a block of mass 5kg on a 30° incline has a component of weight mg sin30° = 5×10×0.5 = 25N down the plane and mg cos30° = 5×10×0.866 = 43.3N normal to the plane. For electromagnetic induction, Faraday's law states that induced EMF = -dΦ/dt where Φ is magnetic flux. Students often struggle with the negative sign, which indicates direction according to Lenz's law.

Class activity:
Students will be grouped according to their identified weaknesses and work through targeted problem sets with the teacher providing additional support and explanations.

Evaluation questions:
1. Resolve the weight of a 10kg block on a 30° incline into components parallel and perpendicular to the plane.
2. Explain Lenz's law and its significance.
3. Calculate the induced EMF in a coil of 100 turns when the magnetic flux through it changes from 0.5Wb to 0.1Wb in 0.2s.
4. Why do students often find nuclear physics calculations challenging?

Summary:
Today's targeted practice has addressed common areas of weakness and improved our problem-solving skills in challenging topics.

topics.title: Final mock
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to demonstrate comprehensive physics knowledge, apply examination techniques effectively, and manage time efficiently during the examination.

Introduction:
As we approach the final week before the WAEC examination, today's full mock will serve as our final practice to ensure we are fully prepared for the actual examination.

Content:
The final mock examination will consist of complete papers covering the entire physics syllabus. The theory paper will include both objective and essay questions, testing recall, comprehension, and problem-solving skills across all topics. Students must demonstrate their ability to draw appropriate diagrams, show clear calculation steps, and provide well-structured answers. The practical paper will require students to set up experiments, take accurate measurements, and present results with proper analysis and error evaluation. Time management is crucial - students should allocate approximately 1 minute per mark for objective questions and 15-20 minutes per essay question.

Class activity:
Students will write a full mock examination under timed conditions, followed by a comprehensive review session where answers are discussed, marking schemes are explained, and common errors are highlighted.

Evaluation questions:
The final mock examination itself serves as the evaluation, with questions covering the entire syllabus and requiring comprehensive knowledge and application skills.

Summary:
Today's final mock examination has provided comprehensive practice for the actual WAEC exam and confirmed our readiness for the examination.

topics.title: WAEC readiness
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to outline effective examination strategies, identify required materials for the examination, and demonstrate confidence in their physics knowledge.

Introduction:
We have completed our revision and practice sessions. Today we will focus on examination strategies and final preparations to ensure success in the WAEC physics examination.

Content:
Effective examination strategy begins with proper preparation. Students should ensure they have all required materials: transparent mathematical set, drawing instruments, and non-programmable calculator. During the examination, careful reading of questions is essential - students should identify key terms and allocate time according to marks. For calculations, students should show all working steps as partial marks may be awarded. For essay questions, answers should be well-structured with clear diagrams where required. Students should also practice good examination hygiene - arriving early, reading instructions carefully, and managing time effectively throughout the examination.

Class activity:
Students will participate in a question-and-answer session addressing any remaining concerns, followed by a motivational talk on examination confidence and stress management techniques.

Evaluation questions:
1. List three items you must bring to the physics examination.
2. Explain how you would manage your time during the examination.
3. Why is showing calculation steps important in physics examinations?
4. Describe how you would approach an essay question on electromagnetic induction.

Summary:
Today's session has equipped you with the strategies and confidence needed to excel in the WAEC physics examination.
